summary: Describes the Layered Coding Transport building block, which provides transport support for reliable content delivery and stream delivery protocols. It is designed for IP multicast but also works with unicast.

plainLanguage.summary: LCT is a common packet format for sending one thing to many receivers at once. It names the session and the object being sent, carries the information a receiver needs to control its own speed, and leaves the job of surviving packet loss to a separate scheme. Receivers never send anything back, which is what makes it scale.

questions: what is the lct header format
how does lct handle congestion control
subtitle: The common packet header for scalable one-to-many content and stream delivery over IP multicast.

tldr.problem: Sending a file to a very large audience over IP multicast fails in two ways: a single lost packet ruins the whole file, and the receivers flood the sender with requests for retransmissions.
tldr.mechanism: LCT defines a packet header with a session identifier, an object identifier and a congestion control field, and it leaves the reliability mechanism to a separate building block such as forward error correction. Receivers never send anything back.
tldr.outcome: A protocol built on LCT can deliver the same content to millions of receivers at different rates, with no feedback and no retransmissions. The document replaced the experimental RFC 3451 in 2009.

today: RFC 5651 is a Proposed Standard on the IETF Standards Track. It replaced RFC 3451 in 2009, allocating the two reserved header bits and moving the timing fields into the EXT_TIME extension, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It is one half of the pair of documents that together define the Asynchronous Layered Coding protocol, whose other half is RFC 5775.

sections.title: What LCT Is For
sections.content:
Layered Coding Transport provides transport level support for reliable content delivery and stream delivery protocols. It is specifically designed to support protocols using IP multicast, but it also supports protocols that use unicast. It is compatible with congestion control that provides multiple rate delivery to receivers, and with coding techniques that provide reliable delivery of content.

The document describes a building block in the sense of RFC 3048: a piece that is meant to be combined with other pieces to make a complete protocol. LCT deliberately avoids functionality that is not massively scalable. It provides no mechanism for sending information from receivers to senders, although that does not rule out protocols that use LCT and do need such feedback.

LCT includes general support for congestion control, which must be used, but does not specify which congestion control to use. The reason is that any protocol that is network friendly has to provide it, and the applications that use LCT differ: a content delivery protocol may want to use all available bandwidth and must back off hard when there is competing traffic, while a streaming protocol may want to hold a steady rate and back off more gently.
sections.plainLanguage: LCT is not a protocol on its own. It is the packet format that a content delivery protocol is built on, and it is deliberately minimal so that nothing in it gets in the way of scaling to millions of receivers.

sections.title: Sessions, Channels and Objects
sections.content:
An LCT session comprises multiple channels originating at a single sender, used for some period of time to carry packets pertaining to the transmission of one or more objects that may interest receivers. The session is defined as originating from a single sender because that is the right granularity at which to regulate packet traffic with congestion control. One reason for several channels in a session is that massively scalable congestion control protocols use multiple channels per session, and they are considered layered because a receiver joins and leaves channels in a layered order during its participation.

An LCT channel is defined by the combination of a sender and an address associated with the channel by the sender. A receiver joins a channel to start receiving the data packets sent to it, and leaves it to stop.

The header carries a Transmission Session ID, which allows a receiver to identify which session a received packet belongs to, which matters because a receiver may be joined to many sessions at once. It also carries a Transport Object Identifier, which says which object the packet carries data about. Header extensions can carry further fields, such as the Sender Current Time, the Expected Residual Time and the Session Last Change time values, and can be used for packet authentication.

LCT is meant to be combined with other building blocks so that the resulting protocol is massively scalable, in the sense of behaviour relative to the number of receivers and network paths, their heterogeneity, and the ability to accommodate a dynamically changing set of receivers.
sections.plainLanguage: One sender runs a session, and the session is split into channels that carry the same data at different rates. Each packet says which session and which file it belongs to, so a receiver can sort them out even when it is in several sessions at once.

sections.title: The LCT Header
sections.content:
Every packet sent to an LCT session must include an LCT header, and its size is variable, given by a length field in the third byte. All integer fields are carried in big-endian, or network order, and bits marked as padding or reserved must be set to zero by senders and ignored by receivers.

The first 32 bits hold the version number V, which is 1 for this specification; the congestion control flag C, which says whether the Congestion Control Information field is 32, 64, 96 or 128 bits long; the Protocol-Specific Indication bits PSI, whose use is up to each protocol instantiation and which must be set to zero and ignored if no use is defined; the Transport Session Identifier flag S; the Transport Object Identifier flag O; the half-word flag H; the two reserved bits; the Close Session flag A and the Close Object flag B; the header length HDR_LEN in units of 32-bit words; and the codepoint CP.

The flags S, O and H together set the lengths of the two identifier fields: the TSI is 32*S + 16*H bits long, so it can be 0, 16, 32 or 48 bits, and the TOI is 32*O + 16*H bits long, so it can be 0, 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96 or 112 bits. The sum of the two lengths is always a multiple of 32 bits.

The TSI uniquely identifies a session among all sessions from a particular sender, and the sender's IP address together with the TSI identifies the session. If the underlying transport is UDP, the 16-bit UDP source port may serve as the TSI. The TOI says which object within the session the packet pertains to, for example a sender sending several files might use TOI=0 for the first and TOI=1 for the second. The codepoint is an opaque identifier passed to the payload decoder, used much like the payload type field in RTP, with the mapping to the actual codec agreed out of band.
sections.plainLanguage: The header starts with a fixed 32 bits that say how long everything else is, then the congestion control information, then the session number and the object number. The session and object numbers can be left out if something else already provides them, such as the UDP port number.

sections.title: Header Extensions
sections.content:
Header extensions carry optional fields that are not always used or have a variable size, such as extended-size versions of existing fields, sender and receiver authentication information, and timing information. Their presence is inferred from the header length: if the length is larger than the standard header, the remaining space holds extensions.

There are two formats. The first is for variable-length extensions, with Header Extension Type values between 0 and 127, and it has a Header Extension Length field giving the length of the whole extension in multiples of 32-bit words. The second is for fixed-length extensions of one 32-bit word, with type values from 128 to 255, and it has no length field; its content is 24 bits. The length of every extension must be a multiple of 32 bits, and the whole LCT header, including all extensions, cannot exceed 255 32-bit words.

Three extensions are defined. EXT_NOP, with type 0, is a no-operation extension whose contents must be ignored. EXT_AUTH, with type 1, carries information used to authenticate the sender of the packet; its format and processing are out of scope and are communicated out of band, and senders are recommended to provide some form of packet authentication. EXT_TIME, with type 2, carries timing information, including the Sender Current Time, the Expected Residual Time and the Session Last Change values, and can also carry timing information of narrower applicability defined elsewhere.

All implementations must support EXT_NOP and must recognise EXT_AUTH and EXT_TIME, though they need not be able to parse their content. Extensions that are not recognised are ignored, which allows backward-compatible extensions without changing the version number.
sections.plainLanguage: Extra fields can be tucked in after the standard header. Each extension has a type number: 0 means ignore it, 1 carries an authenticator, and 2 carries timing information.

sections.title: Congestion Control
sections.content:
Congestion control means adapting the throughput to the bandwidth available on the path from the sender to a receiver, and sharing that bandwidth fairly with competing flows such as TCP. The total flow of packets to each receiver in an LCT session must not compete unfairly with existing flow-adaptive protocols such as TCP. Congestion control that conforms to RFC 2357 must be used between receivers and the sender for each session.

With a multiple rate protocol, a session typically consists of more than one channel, and the sender sends packets to the channels at rates that do not depend on the receivers. Each receiver adjusts its reception rate by joining and leaving channels dynamically, depending on the bandwidth available to it and independently of all other receivers, so each receiver's rate may vary independently of the others.

With a single rate protocol, a session typically consists of one channel and the sender sends packets at variable rates over time, depending on feedback from receivers, while each receiver stays joined to the channel, so the reception rate varies in coordination with all receivers. A multiple rate protocol is generally preferable in a heterogeneous receiver environment, because it more easily scales to many receivers and gives each one a higher throughput; the multiple rate scheme of RFC 3738 is recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: With several channels at different rates, each receiver picks the channels that suit its own connection, so a slow receiver does not hold everyone back. With one channel, the whole group shares the sender's rate.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving
sections.content:
Before joining a session, a receiver must obtain a session description. It must include the sender's IP address, the number of LCT channels, the addresses and port numbers used for each channel, the Transport Session ID to be used, enough information to determine the congestion control protocol in use, and enough information to determine the packet authentication scheme if one is used. It may also include the data rates used for each channel, the length of the packet payload, the mapping of TOI values to objects, and information about each object such as when it will be available and how long it is. The session description could take the form of SDP, or another format, and could be carried by a session announcement protocol, by HTTP, or in any other out-of-band way.

Within a session the sender transmits a sequence of packets over one or more channels. Several objects can be carried in the same session, each identified by a unique TOI, transmitted sequentially or concurrently. The document puts no restriction on packet sizes, but network efficiency considerations recommend as large a payload as possible without exceeding the network's maximum transmission unit, and it recommends that all packets have the same or very similar sizes, because this has a severe impact on the effectiveness of congestion control schemes.

On the receiving side, the behaviour depends on the delivery service model. For an on-demand model, a receiver joins, obtains the packets it needs to reproduce the object, and leaves. For a streaming model, it stays joined to a set of channels throughout. A receiver must be able to process the LCT header, must implement the congestion control protocol named in the session description, and must not join the session if it cannot. When the session uses several channels, receivers must initially join only a minimal set of channels, typically a single one, so that receivers do not all start at high data rates.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver is told how to join before it starts. Then it watches the channels it joined and keeps its own rate under control. A receiver that cannot do the congestion control the session asks for has to stay out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
LCT is a building block and does not define a complete protocol, so protocol instantiations that use it must address the vulnerabilities the document lists. One example of a way to address them is to prevent receivers from accepting incorrect packets, for example with a source authentication and content integrity mechanism.

The document assumes the availability of correct session description information. Incorrect or maliciously modified session description may leave receivers unable to receive the content, or make them try to receive at a much higher rate than they can manage, disrupting traffic in parts of the network. Protocol instantiations must therefore protect the session description, and must let receivers securely check that it corresponds to the LCT data packets.

Several specific fields are called out. Modifying the Transport Session Identifier or the Transport Object Identifier could deprive a session or object of data or send incorrect data elsewhere, and forged packets with fake identifiers could make receivers allocate resources for sessions or objects that do not exist, all of which are denial-of-service risks. The Close Object and Close Session bits have the same kind of risk. The timing fields can be attacked by sending erroneous sender time information or by announcing that a session is about to close. Finally, the protocol-specific bits, the congestion control field, the codepoint and the payload can all be modified to cause a denial of service, for instance by making receivers receive at the wrong rate and worsening congestion. All of these fields must be protected by the protocol instantiation's security mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Because receivers trust what the header says, an attacker who can change it can make them accept the wrong data or request a rate they cannot handle. The document therefore insists that the important header fields are authenticated and checked for tampering.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 3451
sections.content: This document supersedes the experimental RFC 3451 and is based on it, with the changes listed in the document. The statement of intent was removed, and material from ALC that applies to the more general LCT context was included. An IANA registry for LCT header extensions was created. The two reserved bits in the LCT header were allocated as Protocol-Specific Indication, for use to be defined by protocol instantiations. The Sender Current Time and Expected Residual Time header fields were removed, and a new header extension, EXT_TIME, was introduced to replace them and to allow the timing capabilities to be extended later.
sections.plainLanguage: The 2009 version keeps the same packet format but tidies it up: the two spare bits now have a defined purpose, and the timing fields moved into an extension so that more timing information can be added later.

layers.detail: Session, object and congestion control fields

fields.name: V
fields.desc: LCT version number. The value for this specification is 1.

fields.name: C
fields.desc: Congestion control flag: the CCI field is 32, 64, 96 or 128 bits long.

fields.name: PSI
fields.desc: Protocol-Specific Indication, for use defined by each protocol instantiation.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Number of full 32-bit words in the TSI field.

fields.name: O
fields.desc: Number of full 32-bit words in the TOI field.

fields.name: H
fields.desc: Half-word flag: adds 16 bits to the length of the TSI and TOI fields.

fields.name: Res
fields.desc: Reserved. Must be set to zero by senders and ignored by receivers.

fields.name: A
fields.desc: Close Session flag: the sender is about to stop sending for the session.

fields.name: B
fields.desc: Close Object flag: the sender is about to stop sending for the object.

fields.name: HDR_LEN
fields.desc: Total length of the LCT header in units of 32-bit words.

fields.name: CP
fields.desc: Codepoint: an opaque identifier for the codec used on the payload.

items.label: EXT_NOP
items.desc: No-operation extension. Receivers must ignore the contents.

items.label: EXT_AUTH
items.desc: Packet authentication. The format is agreed out of band.

items.label: EXT_TIME
items.desc: Timing information: sender current time, expected residual time and session last change.

viz.caption: TWO WAYS TO CONTROL THE RATE

cells: Sends to the channels at rates that do not depend on the receivers
Sends at variable rates depending on feedback from receivers
Joins and leaves channels dynamically, according to the bandwidth available to it
Stays joined to the channel throughout
May vary independently of the other receivers
